claim: Many current tetrapods use air movement to empower specialized vocal organs such as the larynx of frogs and mammals and the syrinx of birds.
source: Many current tetrapods use air movement to empower specialized vocal organs such as the larynx of frogs and mammals and the syrinx of birds (Elemans et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elemans et al., 2015

claim: Sounds produced by tetrapod vocal organs are shaped by a combination of vibrating elements and cavity resonances to voice different acoustic qualities that convey sex, age, species, emotional state and even intent.
source: The resulting sounds are shaped by a combination of vibrating elements and cavity resonances to voice different acoustic qualities that convey sex, age, species, emotional state and even intent (Hall et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hall et al., 2013

claim: Xenopus is a secondarily aquatic frog genus.
source: Frogs in the secondarily aquatic genus Xenopus (Evans et al., 2015) present an informative system for addressing these questions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Evans et al., 2015

claim: In Xenopus, social communication is dominated by vocal signaling.
source: In Xenopus, social communication is dominated by vocal signaling (Kelley et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelley et al., 2017

claim: Males in each Xenopus species produce distinctive advertisement calls underwater whose acoustic features inform species identity.
source: Males in each species produce distinctive advertisement calls underwater whose acoustic features inform species identity (Evans et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Evans et al., 2015

claim: Xenopus advertisement calls consist of a series of sound pulses that form species-typical temporal patterns and characteristically include two dominant frequencies (DFs).
source: These calls consist of a series of sound pulses that form species-typical temporal patterns and characteristically include two dominant frequencies (DFs) (Hall et al., 2013; Tobias et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hall et al., 2013 and Tobias et al., 2011

claim: Sound pulses that comprise Xenopus calls are produced in the larynx.
source: The sound pulses that comprise Xenopus calls are produced in the larynx, (Tobias and Kelley, 1987) a vocal organ interposed between the nasal and buccal cavities and the lungs (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tobias and Kelley, 1987

claim: Vocal folds are absent in the Xenopus larynx.
source: Vocal folds are absent (Ridewood, 1897) and a separate glottis gates air flow to and from the lungs (Brett and Shelton, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ridewood, 1897

claim: A separate glottis gates air flow to and from the lungs in Xenopus.
source: Vocal folds are absent (Ridewood, 1897) and a separate glottis gates air flow to and from the lungs (Brett and Shelton, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brett and Shelton, 1979

claim: The Xenopus larynx consists of a cricoid frame or 'box' of hyaline cartilage flanked bilaterally by bipennate muscles.
source: The larynx consists of a cricoid frame or 'box' of hyaline cartilage flanked bilaterally by bipennate muscles.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: Laryngeal muscles insert anteriorly, via a tendon, onto paired, closely apposed arytenoid cartilage discs.
source: These insert anteriorly, via a tendon, onto paired, closely apposed arytenoid cartilage discs (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) whose medial faces are coated by mucopolysaccharide secreted by adjacent cells (Yager, 1992).
evidence: Supported by reference to figures and citation to Yager, 1992

claim: The medial faces of arytenoid discs are coated by mucopolysaccharide secreted by adjacent cells.
source: These insert anteriorly, via a tendon, onto paired, closely apposed arytenoid cartilage discs (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) whose medial faces are coated by mucopolysaccharide secreted by adjacent cells (Yager, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yager, 1992

claim: The arytenoid discs are suspended in elastic tissue composed of elastic cartilage and elastin fibrils.
source: The discs are suspended in elastic tissue composed of elastic cartilage and elastin fibrils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Yager, 1992).
evidence: Supported by reference to figure and citation to Yager, 1992

claim: Electrical stimulation of laryngeal muscles or nerves results in species-specific sound pulses, both in situ and ex vivo.
source: Electrical stimulation of laryngeal muscles or nerves results in species-specific sound pulses, both in situ and ex vivo (Yager, 1992; Tobias and Kelley, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yager, 1992 and Tobias and Kelley, 1987

claim: Sound is produced in Xenopus without air flow or vocal folds.
source: Sound is thus produced without air flow or vocal folds.
evidence: Inference based on previous statements about laryngeal structure and function

claim: In X. borealis, separations of the paired arytenoid discs accompany sound pulses.
source: In X. borealis, separations of the paired arytenoid discs accompany sound pulses, (Yager, 1992) but how disc motion results in sound production has not been resolved.
evidence: Supported by citation to Yager, 1992

claim: The mechanism by which disc motion results in sound production has not been resolved.
source: In X. borealis, separations of the paired arytenoid discs accompany sound pulses, (Yager, 1992) but how disc motion results in sound production has not been resolved.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field

claim: Cavitation is the currently accepted hypothesis for underwater laryngeal sound production in Xenopus.
source: An unusual mechanism – implosion of air bubbles or cavitation (Yager, 1992) - is the currently accepted (Irisarri et al., 2011; Ladich and Winkler, 2017) hypothesis for underwater laryngeal sound production in Xenopus.
evidence: Supported by citations to Yager, 1992; Irisarri et al., 2011; Ladich and Winkler, 2017

claim: According to the cavitation hypothesis, high velocity separation of the arytenoid discs causes formation of bubbles that then implode and produce sounds.
source: In this scenario, the high velocity separation of the arytenoid discs causes formation of bubbles that then implode and produce sounds.
evidence: Description of the cavitation hypothesis

claim: Cavitation bubbles are known to produce hydrodynamic propeller noise.
source: Cavitation bubbles are known to produce hydrodynamic propeller noise (Carlton, 2012) and the 'snaps' of some species of shrimp (Versluis et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carlton, 2012

claim: Cavitation bubbles produce the 'snaps' of some species of shrimp.
source: Cavitation bubbles are known to produce hydrodynamic propeller noise (Carlton, 2012) and the 'snaps' of some species of shrimp (Versluis et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Versluis et al., 2000

claim: The small film of fluid between the arytenoid discs should allow neither high velocity flow nor bubble formation.
source: The small film of fluid between the arytenoid discs should allow neither high velocity flow nor bubble formation, and bubbles have not yet been observed.
evidence: Reasoning based on physical constraints

claim: Bubbles have not yet been observed between arytenoid discs.
source: The small film of fluid between the arytenoid discs should allow neither high velocity flow nor bubble formation, and bubbles have not yet been observed.
evidence: Statement of observational fact

claim: Cavitation bubble collapse produces a high amplitude pressure pulse (~50–100 kPa), several orders of magnitude louder than the radiated sound pressure of Xenopus sound pulses.
source: Additionally, cavitation bubble collapse produces a high amplitude pressure pulse (~50–100 kPa), several orders of magnitude louder than the radiated sound pressure of Xenopus sound pulses.
evidence: Comparison based on established knowledge of cavitation and observed Xenopus sound pressures

claim: The duration of pressure transients produced by the collapse of cavitation bubbles are in the microsecond range, rather than the millisecond range of Xenopus sound pulses.
source: Finally, the duration of pressure transients produced by the collapse of cavitation bubbles are in the microsecond range, rather than the millisecond range of Xenopus sound pulses.
evidence: Comparison based on established knowledge of cavitation and observed Xenopus sound pulse durations

claim: Disc movements accompanied sound production in isolated X. laevis larynges during sound pulse production evoked by stimulation of the laryngeal nerve.
source: As reported previously, (Yager, 1992) disc movements accompanied sound production (Figure 1C,E,F; Video 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yager, 1992 and reference to figures and video

claim: Nerve stimulation first produces isometric contraction of the bipennate muscles during which the arytenoid discs remain apposed.
source: Nerve stimulation first produces isometric contraction of the bipennate muscles during which the arytenoid discs remain apposed.
evidence: Direct observation from experimental data

claim: A fluid layer could be observed retreating from the medial surface of the discs with increasing isometric force.
source: In favorable preparations, a fluid layer could then be observed retreating from the medial surface of the discs with increasing isometric force.
evidence: Direct observation from experimental data

claim: The discs are kept together by a capillary binding force through a liquid bridge.
source: This observation suggests that the discs are kept together by a capillary binding force through a liquid bridge.
evidence: Inference from observation of fluid layer behavior

claim: When bilaterally exerted muscle force overcomes the binding force, the liquid bridge ruptures and the discs separate rapidly.
source: When bilaterally exerted muscle force overcomes the binding force, the liquid bridge ruptures (Figure 1F) and the discs separate rapidly with mean gap peak acceleration of 13.5 ± 9.1 g (N = 3; range: 6.4–23.8 g, where 1 g = 9.82 m/s2) and mean peak velocity of 50.3 ± 21.9 mm/s (N = 3; range: 35.5–75.4 mm/s) (see examples: Figure 1E; Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements and figures

claim: Mean gap peak acceleration during disc separation is 13.5 ± 9.1 g (N = 3; range: 6.4–23.8 g).
source: When bilaterally exerted muscle force overcomes the binding force, the liquid bridge ruptures (Figure 1F) and the discs separate rapidly with mean gap peak acceleration of 13.5 ± 9.1 g (N = 3; range: 6.4–23.8 g, where 1 g = 9.82 m/s2) and mean peak velocity of 50.3 ± 21.9 mm/s (N = 3; range: 35.5–75.4 mm/s) (see examples: Figure 1E; Figure 2B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experiments

claim: Mean peak velocity during disc separation is 50.3 ± 21.9 mm/s (N = 3; range: 35.5–75.4 mm/s).
source: When bilaterally exerted muscle force overcomes the binding force, the liquid bridge ruptures (Figure 1F) and the discs separate rapidly with mean gap peak acceleration of 13.5 ± 9.1 g (N = 3; range: 6.4–23.8 g, where 1 g = 9.82 m/s2) and mean peak velocity of 50.3 ± 21.9 mm/s (N = 3; range: 35.5–75.4 mm/s) (see examples: Figure 1E; Figure 2B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experiments

claim: Disc peak deceleration (10.6 ± 5.2 g; N = 3; range: 6.5–16.4 g) occurs only 0.57 ± 0.10 ms after peak acceleration.
source: Disc peak deceleration (10.6 ± 5.2 g; N = 3; range: 6.5–16.4 g) occurs only 0.57 ± 0.10 ms after peak acceleration.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experiments

claim: In 0.57 ± 0.10 ms after peak acceleration, the gap between the discs enlarges to 18.6 ± 5.5 µm (range: 14.1–24.8 µm).
source: In this short time, the gap between the discs enlarges to 18.6 ± 5.5 µm (range: 14.1–24.8 µm), a value that is 27.5 ± 8.0% (range: 22.8–35.6%) of the maximum gap width of 72.6 ± 34.5 µm (N = 3; range: 39.6–108.4 µm).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experiments

claim: The gap enlargement of 18.6 ± 5.5 µm is 27.5 ± 8.0% (range: 22.8–35.6%) of the maximum gap width of 72.6 ± 34.5 µm (N = 3; range: 39.6–108.4 µm).
source: In this short time, the gap between the discs enlarges to 18.6 ± 5.5 µm (range: 14.1–24.8 µm), a value that is 27.5 ± 8.0% (range: 22.8–35.6%) of the maximum gap width of 72.6 ± 34.5 µm (N = 3; range: 39.6–108.4 µm).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experiments

claim: Peak acceleration precedes sound onset by 0.85 ± 0.33 ms.
source: Peak acceleration and velocity precede sound onsets by 0.85 ± 0.33 and 0.51 ± 0.33 ms respectively (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experiments with figure reference

claim: Peak velocity precedes sound onset by 0.51 ± 0.33 ms.
source: Peak acceleration and velocity precede sound onsets by 0.85 ± 0.33 and 0.51 ± 0.33 ms respectively (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experiments with figure reference

claim: The interval between disc acceleration and velocity shows less variation (0.34 ± 0.06 ms, N = 3) than the interval between disc separation and sound radiation.
source: The delay (Figure 1F) between disc acceleration and velocity shows less variation (0.34 ± 0.06 ms, N = 3) indicating that sound onset timing after disc separation, rather than disc kinematics, is more variable between preparations.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experiments with figure reference

claim: Sound onset timing after disc separation, rather than disc kinematics, is more variable between preparations.
source: The delay (Figure 1F) between disc acceleration and velocity shows less variation (0.34 ± 0.06 ms, N = 3) indicating that sound onset timing after disc separation, rather than disc kinematics, is more variable between preparations.
evidence: Inference from comparison of variability measurements

claim: At 40 Hz nerve stimulation rates, the first few stimuli do not result in sound pulse production.
source: At 40 Hz nerve stimulation rates (within natural call sound pulse rates (Tobias et al., 2011)), the first few stimuli do not result in sound pulse production (Figure 2A).
evidence: Observation from experimental data with figure reference

claim: Male laryngeal neuromuscular synapses are 'weak,' i.e., require facilitation to release sufficient neurotransmitter to generate a muscle action potential and contraction.
source: This corroborates previous results that male laryngeal neuromuscular synapses are 'weak,' i.e., require facilitation to release sufficient neurotransmitter to generate a muscle action potential and contraction (Tobias and Kelley, 1987; Ruel et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tobias and Kelley, 1987 and Ruel et al., 1997

claim: Over multiple stimulations, peak-to-peak (ptp) sound pressure increases linearly with both peak velocity and acceleration.
source: Subsequently, over multiple stimulations, peak-to-peak (ptp) sound pressure increases linearly with both peak velocity and acceleration and reaches a maximum received level of ~180 mPa ptp (at 44 mm) in all preparations (Figure 2B).
evidence: Observation from experimental data with figure reference

claim: Peak-to-peak sound pressure reaches a maximum received level of ~180 mPa ptp (at 44 mm) in all preparations.
source: Subsequently, over multiple stimulations, peak-to-peak (ptp) sound pressure increases linearly with both peak velocity and acceleration and reaches a maximum received level of ~180 mPa ptp (at 44 mm) in all preparations (Figure 2B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experiments with figure reference

claim: Below a minimal peak velocity of 28 ± 12 mm/s, no sound is detected.
source: Below a minimal peak velocity of 28 ± 12 mm/s and minimal peak acceleration of 4.6 ± 3.1 g, no sound is detected, suggesting a threshold disc velocity or acceleration required to produce sound.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experiments

claim: Below a minimal peak acceleration of 4.6 ± 3.1 g, no sound is detected.
source: Below a minimal peak velocity of 28 ± 12 mm/s and minimal peak acceleration of 4.6 ± 3.1 g, no sound is detected, suggesting a threshold disc velocity or acceleration required to produce sound.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experiments

claim: A threshold disc velocity or acceleration is required to produce sound.
source: Below a minimal peak velocity of 28 ± 12 mm/s and minimal peak acceleration of 4.6 ± 3.1 g, no sound is detected, suggesting a threshold disc velocity or acceleration required to produce sound.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: When water was introduced via the glottis into the supradisc space, no sound was produced.
source: When water was introduced via the glottis into the supradisc space, no sound was produced, corroborating earlier observations in X. borealis (Yager, 1992).
evidence: Experimental observation corroborated by citation to Yager, 1992

claim: Of disc gap width, peak velocity and peak acceleration, only disc peak velocity does not reach threshold when the liquid bridge holding the discs together is disrupted.
source: Of disc gap width, peak velocity and peak acceleration, only disc peak velocity does not reach threshold when the liquid bridge holding the discs together is disrupted (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from experimental data with figure reference

claim: A threshold disc peak velocity is required for sound production.
source: This observation supports the hypothesis that a threshold disc peak velocity is required for sound production.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: Three sets of observations do not support the cavitation hypothesis: (1) no bubble formation is observed, (2) sound pressures are six orders of magnitude too low (mPa vs kPa), and (3) the onset of sound production is three orders of magnitude too slow (ms vs µs).
source: In summary, three sets of observations do not support the cavitation hypothesis: (1) we do not observe bubble formation, (2) sound pressures are six orders of magnitude too low (mPa vs kPa), and (3) the onset of sound production is three orders of magnitude too slow (ms vs µs).
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Sound pulses produced ex vivo in male X. laevis larynges include species-specific frequencies also present in actual calls.
source: We have previously reported (Tobias and Kelley, 1987) that sound pulses produced ex vivo in male X. laevis larynges include species-specific frequencies also present in actual calls.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tobias and Kelley, 1987

claim: In the three clades of Xenopus sub-genus - L, M and A - each repeated sound pulse in the male advertisement call has two simultaneously produced frequency bands: a higher dominant frequency (DF2) and a lower frequency (DF1), termed dyads.
source: In the three clades of this sub-genus - L (which includes X. laevis), M (which includes X. borealis) and A (which includes X. andrei and X. amieti) (Evans et al., 2015) - each repeated sound pulse in the male advertisement call has two simultaneously produced frequency bands: a higher dominant frequency (DF2) and a lower frequency (DF1) (Tobias et al., 2011), termed dyads (Figure 3A,C,D).
evidence: Supported by citations and figure references

claim: All but one Xenopus species produce advertisement calls made up of harmonic dyads in which DF1 and DF2 are related by a small-integer ratio.
source: All but one species produce advertisement calls made up of harmonic dyads in which DF1 and DF2 are related by a small-integer ratio.
evidence: Observation from analysis of call recordings

claim: X. allofraseri is the exception in which pulses contain harmonic stacks rather than harmonic dyads.
source: The exception is X. allofraseri in which pulses contain harmonic stacks.
evidence: Observation from analysis of call recordings

claim: There is a broad range for both the lower and the higher dominant frequency across Xenopus.
source: There is a broad range for both the lower and the higher dominant frequency across Xenopus (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Observation from data shown in figures

claim: Either DF1 or DF2 can be shared by different Xenopus species.
source: Either DF1 or DF2 can be shared by different species.
evidence: Observation from analysis of call recordings

claim: The ratio of DF2/DF1 is specific to, and highly conserved within, each Xenopus clade.
source: However, in contrast to individual frequencies, the ratio of DF2/DF1 is specific to, and highly conserved within, each clade (Figure 3E).
evidence: Observation from analysis of call recordings with figure reference

claim: The mean DF2/DF1 ratio for A clade species is 1.33 (±0.004).
source: The mean ratio (Table 1) for A clade species is 1.33 (±0.004), for L clade species is 1.23 (±0.020), and for M clade species is 2.02 (±0.032).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from call analysis

claim: The mean DF2/DF1 ratio for L clade species is 1.23 (±0.020).
source: The mean ratio (Table 1) for A clade species is 1.33 (±0.004), for L clade species is 1.23 (±0.020), and for M clade species is 2.02 (±0.032).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from call analysis

claim: The mean DF2/DF1 ratio for M clade species is 2.02 (±0.032).
source: The mean ratio (Table 1) for A clade species is 1.33 (±0.004), for L clade species is 1.23 (±0.020), and for M clade species is 2.02 (±0.032).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from call analysis

claim: X. wittei in the A clade has a DF2/DF1 ratio of 1.19, not 1.34, making it an exception.
source: Exceptions include X. wittei in the A clade (1.19, not 1.34) and X. laevis South Africa in the L clade (1.14, not 1.24).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from call analysis

claim: X. laevis South Africa in the L clade has a DF2/DF1 ratio of 1.14, not 1.24, making it an exception.
source: Exceptions include X. wittei in the A clade (1.19, not 1.34) and X. laevis South Africa in the L clade (1.14, not 1.24).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from call analysis

claim: Species in different clades can share either DF1 or DF2 but not the distinctive ratio.
source: Thus, species in different clades can share either DF1 or DF2 but not the distinctive ratio.
evidence: Inference from analysis of call recordings

claim: A singing male and an isolated larynx with intact elastic cartilage septa produce the same dyad in sound and laser recordings.
source: A singing male and an isolated larynx with intact elastic cartilage septa produce the same dyad in sound and laser recordings (A) Recordings from a X. boumbaensis male. Spectrograph (frequency vs time) of one pulse obtained from sound and laser vibrometry recordings. At right: Power spectra from the sound (grey) and laser (black) spectrographs. (B) Recordings from the isolated larynx of a X. boumbaensis male. Spectrograph (frequency vs time) of one pulse obtained from sound and laser vibrometry recordings, At right: Power spectra from the sound (grey) and laser (black) spectrographs.
evidence: Experimental observation with figure reference

claim: The dyads reported are produced by the frog.
source: The same dyad was present in both sounds and vibrations from a vocalizing male (Figure 4A). Thus, the dyads reported here are produced by the frog.
evidence: Experimental observation with figure reference

claim: Isolated larynges produced the same dyads as the intact animal.
source: To determine whether dyads are produced solely by the larynx (without contributions from other organs), we recorded sound and vibrations produced by isolated larynges in response to nerve stimulation (Figure 4B). Isolated larynges produced the same dyads as the intact animal.
evidence: Experimental observation with figure reference

claim: The generation of dyads is intrinsic to the larynx and is not influenced by extra-laryngeal tissues.
source: Thus, the generation of dyads is intrinsic to the larynx and is not influenced by extra-laryngeal tissues.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: The interior of the Xenopus larynx includes a central, air-filled chamber (C) separated from smaller, lateral chambers (L) by elastic cartilage septa.
source: The interior of the larynx (Figure 4C) includes a central, air-filled chamber (C) separated from smaller, lateral chambers (L) by elastic cartilage septa (Figure 4C, inset).
evidence: Observation from histological sections with figure reference

claim: Puncturing the elastic cartilage either abolished the DF peaks by shifting the two narrowly tuned bands to a single, intermediate, broader band frequency (5/12 larynges), abolished one peak and broadened the other (2/12), abolished both peaks (4/12) or shifted peaks to a different ratio (1/12).
source: However, puncturing the elastic cartilage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) either abolished the DF peaks by shifting the two narrowly tuned bands to a single, intermediate, broader band frequency (5/12 larynges; Figure 4D), abolished one peak and broadened the other (2/12), abolished both peaks (4/12) or shifted peaks to a different ratio (1/12).
evidence: Experimental observation with figure reference

claim: In X. borealis, 'opening' the cricoid box by removing a rectangular portion of the ventral laryngeal wall detunes the larynx.
source: In X. borealis, 'opening' the cricoid box by removing a rectangular portion of the ventral laryngeal wall detunes the larynx (Yager, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yager, 1992

claim: The detuning from opening the cricoid box could have been due to disruption of elastic cartilages.
source: This detuning could also have been due to disruption of elastic cartilages.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: The puncture of elastic cartilage created a single air space.
source: Because the elastic cartilage partitions the internal air chambers of the larynx, the puncture created a single air space.
evidence: Inference from anatomical structure and experimental manipulation

claim: The data do not support the prevailing cavitation hypothesis for sound production in Xenopus.
source: Our data do not support the prevailing (Yager, 1992; Irisarri et al., 2011; Ladich and Winkler, 2017) cavitation hypothesis for sound production in Xenopus.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental findings with citations

claim: Two alternative mechanisms that could account for the association between disc movement and sound production are: 1) acoustic excitation by a rapid pressure drop between the discs or 2) disc movement-associated mechanical excitation of the larynx.
source: Two alternative mechanisms that could account for the association between disc movement and sound production are: 1) acoustic excitation by a rapid pressure drop between the discs or 2) disc movement-associated mechanical excitation of the larynx.
evidence: Speculation about alternative mechanisms

claim: Sound pressure reduction between the discs may produce a propagating sound pressure wave, exciting air cavity resonances within the larynx.
source: Sound pressure reduction between the discs may produce a propagating sound pressure wave, exciting air cavity resonances within the larynx.
evidence: Speculation about mechanism

claim: The acoustic excitation mechanism should result in a bipole sound source with strong directional radiation pattern.
source: This mechanism should result in a bipole sound source with strong directional radiation pattern (Larsen and Wahlberg, 2017).
evidence: Inference based on physics with citation

claim: Because of impedance mismatch between the air cavities and cartilages of the larynx, the acoustic excitation mechanism would produce a poor, low intensity sound.
source: Because of impedance mismatch between the air cavities and cartilages of the larynx, however, this mechanism would produce a poor, low intensity sound.
evidence: Inference based on physics

claim: Replacing air with helium should alter the frequency distribution of cavity resonances.
source: In addition, replacing air with helium should alter the frequency distribution of cavity resonances (Rand and Dudley, 1993), an effect not observed in this study, nor previously (Yager, 1992).
evidence: Inference based on physics with citations

claim: Replacing air with helium did not alter the frequency distribution in this study or previously.
source: In addition, replacing air with helium should alter the frequency distribution of cavity resonances (Rand and Dudley, 1993), an effect not observed in this study, nor previously (Yager, 1992).
evidence: Experimental observation with citation

claim: Separation of the arytenoid discs might mechanically excite vibration of laryngeal elements.
source: Alternatively, separation of the arytenoid discs might mechanically excite vibration of laryngeal elements.
evidence: Speculation about alternative mechanism

claim: The mechanical excitation mechanism would result in a monopole sound source – the entire larynx - with a more omnidirectional radiation pattern, effectively coupled to the medium, producing a more intense sound.
source: This mechanism would result in a monopole sound source – the entire larynx - with a more omnidirectional radiation pattern, effectively coupled to the medium, producing a more intense sound.
evidence: Inference based on physics

claim: The sound pressure produced by a vibrating monopole structure depends on its space and time averaged velocity.
source: The sound pressure produced by such a vibrating monopole structure depends on its space and time averaged velocity (Hambric and Fahnline, 2007), which is consistent with our observations of a linear correlation between disc velocity and sound pressure, and the minimal velocity required for sound production.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hambric and Fahnline, 2007

claim: The mechanical excitation mechanism is consistent with observations of a linear correlation between disc velocity and sound pressure, and the minimal velocity required for sound production.
source: The sound pressure produced by such a vibrating monopole structure depends on its space and time averaged velocity (Hambric and Fahnline, 2007), which is consistent with our observations of a linear correlation between disc velocity and sound pressure, and the minimal velocity required for sound production.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: The mechanical excitation mechanism is consistent with previous experiments in which splitting 'the elastic sac surrounding the discs' prevented sound pulse production.
source: This mechanism is also consistent with previous experiments in which splitting 'the elastic sac surrounding the discs' (Yager, 1992) prevented sound pulse production.
evidence: Supported by citation to Yager, 1992

claim: The authors favor the mechanical excitation mechanism and propose that disc movements specifically excite vibration of the elastic tissues surrounding the discs.
source: We thus favor the second explanation and propose that disc movements specifically excite vibration of the elastic tissues surrounding the discs (illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Conclusion from experimental findings with figure reference

claim: Key features of the Xenopus larynx - including lack of vocal folds and modification of the laryngeal box and cartilages - are shared across Pipid species.
source: As key features of the Xenopus larynx - including lack of vocal folds and modification of the laryngeal box and cartilages - are shared across Pipid species (Ridewood, 1897; Ridewood, 1900), this proposed mechanism of underwater sound production may also be shared.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ridewood, 1897 and Ridewood, 1900

claim: The proposed mechanism of underwater sound production may be shared across Pipid species.
source: As key features of the Xenopus larynx - including lack of vocal folds and modification of the laryngeal box and cartilages - are shared across Pipid species (Ridewood, 1897; Ridewood, 1900), this proposed mechanism of underwater sound production may also be shared.
evidence: Inference from shared anatomical features

claim: In Xenopus, water is prevented from entering the larynx during underwater calling by inhibition of glottal motor neurons.
source: In Xenopus, water is prevented from entering the larynx during underwater calling by inhibition of glottal motor neurons (Zornik and Kelley, 2007), thus ensuring the attainment of the disc peak velocity values identified here as required for sound production.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zornik and Kelley, 2007

claim: Inhibition of glottal motor neurons ensures the attainment of the disc peak velocity values required for sound production.
source: In Xenopus, water is prevented from entering the larynx during underwater calling by inhibition of glottal motor neurons (Zornik and Kelley, 2007), thus ensuring the attainment of the disc peak velocity values identified here as required for sound production.
evidence: Inference from experimental findings and cited work

claim: Hymenochirus merlini has reverted to calling in air.
source: The sound-protection afforded would not be required in another pipid, Hymenochirus merlini, that has reverted to calling in air (Irisarri et al., 2011), presumably through an open glottis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Irisarri et al., 2011

claim: H. merlini presumably calls through an open glottis.
source: The sound-protection afforded would not be required in another pipid, Hymenochirus merlini, that has reverted to calling in air (Irisarri et al., 2011), presumably through an open glottis.
evidence: Speculation based on inference

claim: The authors predict that H. merlini calling is also powered by disc separation rather than air flow.
source: We predict that H. merlini calling is also powered by disc separation rather than air flow.
evidence: Prediction based on inference from shared anatomy

claim: Arytenoid disc movements excite two natural vibratory resonance frequencies of the larynx itself.
source: Our experimental results support the hypothesis that arytenoid disc movements subsequently excite two natural vibratory resonance frequencies of the larynx itself.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental findings

claim: Harmonic dyads require intact elastic cartilage septa that separate the central laryngeal lumen from the lateral laryngeal chambers.
